entry.title: The Evolution of Graphical User Interface Design
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | youtube.com | discussion

Mid-century innovations such as the trackball and Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad laid the groundwork for the Graphical User Interface (GUI). Douglas Engelbart’s 1968 "Mother of All Demos" significantly advanced the field by demonstrating the mouse, hyperlinks, and word processing, while subsequent work at Xerox PARC through Smalltalk and the desktop metaphor established the framework for modern computing.

The implementation of the "WIMP" (Windows, Icons, Menu, Pointer) model replaced text-based command interfaces with a skeuomorphic representation of a physical workspace. While research at MIT and Xerox PARC provided the fundamental technology, the commercialization of these ideas by companies like Apple moved the interface into the consumer mainstream. This shift transitioned computers from specialized mathematical tools into intuitive, personal devices.

entry.content:

Currently, the kernel offloads these operations to worker threads to prevent blocking the caller, incurring context-switching costs even when operations complete without blocking. entry.title: Why Mutable and Immutable Types Are Not Subtypes
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | crumbles.blog | discussion

Mutable and immutable types cannot share a subtype relationship without violating the Liskov Substitution Principle. An immutable type cannot be substituted for a mutable one because it lacks mutation operations, and a mutable type cannot be substituted for an immutable one because it fails to uphold the guarantee of value stability required for operations like hash consing.

Languages accommodate these distinct types through ad hoc polymorphism, such as type classes, interfaces, or traits in statically typed systems. In dynamic languages, duck typing is commonly used to allow different types to respond to similar operations, though this can complicate reasoning about type safety and data flow.

jemalloc version 5.4.0 has been released, featuring over 160 commits focused on technical debt reduction, refactoring, and bug fixes. entry.title: Wax Motor Mechanism and Applications
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | en.wikipedia.org | hacker news

These linear actuators convert thermal energy into mechanical energy by exploiting the volume expansion of wax during its phase change. A typical device consists of an enclosed volume of wax, a plunger to convert hydraulic force into mechanical output, and both a heat source and a heat sink.

These actuators can operate passively by matching wax melting points to ambient temperature ranges and provide significant hydraulic force. They are utilized in aerospace controls, HVAC thermostatic valves, washing machine door locks, and greenhouse ventilation systems.

entry.content:
Hacker News Best | bend-lang.com | hacker news

Bend is a high-performance programming language that uses formal proofs to ensure AI-generated code adheres to specific constraints. Through its BendTT affine dependent type theory, developers can define "laws" that the compiler verifies as mathematical theorems, effectively blocking logic errors that would otherwise be introduced by AI agents during code generation.

The language offers Python-like syntax and is designed for massive parallelism, capable of running on both CPUs and GPUs through the BendRT runtime. This approach aims to bridge the gap between natural language intent and executable code, providing a fast and verifiable way to build applications in an AI-centric development environment.
